items.note: Lists Udayapura among the few towns worth mentioning that rose to importance in the Paramara period (alongside Bhilsa, Dhara, Ujjain); Ganguly's table.
Malwa population described as Brahmans, Ksatriyas, Kayasthas, Vaisyas, Sudras and Tailakas, the Brahmana highest (general Paramara-period Malwa).
Paramara kings were Ksatriyas and formed social relations with ruling dynasties by intermarriage.
Udayaditya's daughter (sentence begins on previous page) was married to a Guhila king; further Paramara marriage alliances follow.
Villages and cities had markets, traders' associations and a list of chief articles for sale in Paramara Malwa.
Gold coins apparently of Udayaditya's reign found in the Central Provinces, similar to those of Kalacuri Gangeyadeva; obverse legend Srimad-Udayadeva.
Even as Paramara government was near extinction its forces numbered thirty or forty thousand cavalry; Paramaras noted for elephant forces.
Paramara kings were devout worshippers of Siva; Udayaditya built a temple to Siva at Udayapur.
Names of Siva worshipped, including Nilakanthesvara and Udalesvara.
Visvesvara Sambhu established many Saiva monasteries in central and southern India; Malava kings said to be his disciples.
Images bathed and anointed; worship by sacrificing holy wood, kusa, sesamum and rice in the fire, with food and flowers offered.
Caste system at the basis of Hindu society; Udayaditya and Naravarman declared their swords ever ready to protect varna.
Numerous Hindu monasteries fostered study; Saiva monastery Natana in Ujjain.
Bhava Brhaspati, Superintendent of Saiva temples at Dhara, wrote on the Siva cult; Paramara kings became his disciples.
Vasantotsava (Spring Festival) as the chief ceremony, with other observances such as Diwali and eclipses.
Bhoja said to lean towards Jainism through Dhanapala, yet devoted to the Brahmanical faith to the end of his life.
Merutunga's account of Bhoja's convention of sects; author infers Bhoja followed a policy of toleration (no other evidence corroborates the report).
Naravarman favourably disposed to Jainism and drawn to Samudraghosa for his learning.
Jainas never attained predominance over the Brahmanical religion under Paramara rule; Mahakala temple flag raised over Jain flags.
Paramara kings great builders of cities, lakes and temples; Bhoja rebuilt Dhara.
Remains of Bhojpur, tradition ascribes its foundation to Bhoja; the Bhojpur lake once the greatest of its kind in India.
Kincaid's description of the Bhojpur lake dams; the surviving dam still turns the Kaliasot river into the Betwa.
King Udayaditya founded the city of Udayapur, thirty miles north of Bhilsa.
Legend of the king, the snake surrounded by fire and the king's illness leading to the halt at the village that became Udayapur.

claim.value: legend: Udayaditya founded city after snake episode

items.note: Legend continued: halt at the tiny village, the two snakes overheard speaking about oil and pepper, salt and buttermilk remedies.
Legend concludes: king takes the treasure and builds a city and temple named after himself.
The story is called an absolute myth; a contemporary inscription shows the city was built by Udayaditya; Udayapur now only a small village with traces of ancient glory.

claim.value: built by Udayaditya (contemporary inscription); snake story a myth

items.note: Udayasamudra, attributed by an early record to Udayaditya, cannot now be traced.

claim.value: attributed to Udayaditya; cannot now be traced

refs: Prog. Rep. Arch. Survey, Western Circle, 1914, p. 66

items.note: Udayapur prasasti says Bhoja covered the world with temples (Kedaresvara, Ramesvara, Somanatha etc.); author concludes all were built in Malwa.
Nilakanthesvara temple at Udayapur built by Udayaditya in Sam 1116 = 1059 AD.
A sixteenth-century inscription describes the temple as the most beautiful in India; one of the few Malwa temples spared complete demolition.
Legend: Muhammad Tughluq ordered the temple blown up; priests let water in and the order was revoked; a Veda hall became a mosque.

claim.value: Tughluq's gunpowder neutralised by priests' water; order revoked

items.note: Tradition: Aurangzeb halted at Udayapur, ordered destruction, but Mahadeva appeared in a dream and struck him ill; he rescinded.

claim.value: Aurangzeb relented after dream and illness

items.note: Temple still perfect, hard fine-grained red sandstone, in a paved courtyard, shrine and hall with three porches.
Hall: central Nandi under domed ceiling, eight pillars and four pilasters, pyramidal roof of overlapping stones.
Tower compared to Gondesvara at Sinnar and Ambaranatha; differs from Khajuraho groups; four bands, thirty-five miniature sikharas each, amalakasila and vase.

claim.value: like Gondesvara (Sinnar) and Ambaranatha; unlike Khajuraho

items.note: Figure below amalakasila probably Udayaditya holding a flag-staff; an inscription records he repaired the flag-staff in 1080 AD.
refs: Beglar's Report, ASI Vol. VII, p. 86

items.note: Entrance door with five jambs each side, floral designs, horsemen on outermost jambs, Ganesa and Siva on lintel, five goddesses on frieze.
Beglar and Fergusson assessments of the temple's floral ornament and perfection.
refs: Fergusson, Indian and Eastern Architecture II p. 147

items.note: A vedi in front, said to have been built by the king for a sacrifice after completion; a square chamber with stone screens.
Four subordinate temples at the courtyard corners and four square vedis for reading Vedas mid-sides.
Muhammad Tugluq razed the north-east corner temple and a Veda hall, built a mosque with two inscriptions dated Hijra 737 and 739.
Each Veda-reading hall: square with four pillars, overlapping-stone ceiling, four balconies with a seat slab for the reader.
Un an important Paramara centre of architectural activity; an inscription of Udayaditya (1059-1086) dates its temples.
Udayaditya's inscription at Un's Chaubara Dera with a sarpa-bandha (intertwined snakes), similar to that at Bhoja's school at Dhara.
Miniature sikharas on Gaolesvara like Parsvanatha at Khajuraha, said to be less conventional than those on the Nilakanthesvara temple at Udayapur.

items.note: Bijamandira at Bhilsa, a mosque that is a converted Hindu temple; pillar inscription of Naravarman's reign records devotion to Carcika.
Inscription of Udayaditya's reign (i.e. Udayavarman) dated Saka 1103 found inserted in the wall of the Bijamandira.
Bhojasala at Dhar bears inscriptions of Bhoja, Arjunavarman, Udayaditya and Naravarman and a chart of the Sanskrit alphabet and grammar.
